html:
Open the page and the splash gives way to the workbench. It is laid out like Logix Designer because the habits transfer: the Controller Organizer on the left, document tabs across the middle, the Errors / Simulator Log / Search Results / Cross Reference / Watch panes at the bottom, and a status bar under everything.

In the app

Help → Take the Tour (or Take the tour on the Start Page) walks the same ground in two minutes on your own screen: the tabs, the logic and the simulator, one highlighted piece at a time. The arrow keys step through it.

The title bar, the toolbar and the key switch

Under the menus is the standard toolbar: New, Open and Save; Verify; the Toggle button for the bit you have selected in the ladder; Rung, Edit Rung, Comment and Delete Rung; Undo and Redo; the E-STOP; and Move Rung Up and Down.

Below the toolbar on the left is the controller status: the key switch, Forces, Edits, Controller OK, Energy Storage OK, I/O OK, and the path (AB_ETHIP-1\192.168.1.20\Backplane\0) with whether the controller is online and scanning. The key switch reads the way Logix Designer reads it — Rem Prog, Rem Run, Rem Test — and the same switch sits on the simulator’s own header as Running — click for Program Mode and back. In Program mode inputs still update (you can watch a sensor change in Monitor Tags) but the ladder does not run and outputs are off. In Run mode the ladder scans and outputs drive the machine. Test mode scans without energising outputs.

The E-STOP does what the operator’s E-Stop and the key switch do together: every Emergency Stop in the scene is pressed and latched — the program sees its OK contact drop, and the Simulator Log says which — and the controller goes to Program mode, so outputs are off whatever the program does with the E-Stop. The button stays down; press it again to twist the E-Stops out, then choose Run Mode to start again. Without an E-Stop in the scene it is still the hard stop.

The menus

Every menu, as it reads in v2.02:

  • File — New Project…, New Controller (clear tags and rungs)…, Open… Ctrl+O, Save Ctrl+S, Save As… Ctrl+Shift+S, Export / Copy as Text…, Share Link…, Open Link…, Import L5X (Studio 5000)…, Export L5X (Studio 5000)…, Load Reference Solution: Complete Bottle Line (15 steps), Load Reference Solution.
  • Edit — Undo Ctrl+Z, Redo Ctrl+Y, Cut Ctrl+X, Copy Ctrl+C, Paste Ctrl+V, Paste Before Ctrl+Shift+V, Find… Ctrl+F, Find Next F3, Replace… Ctrl+H, Go To… Ctrl+G, Cross Reference… Ctrl+E, Add Rung Ins, Edit Rung Enter, Add Rung Comment Ctrl+D, Delete Rung Comment, Delete Rung Del, Move Rung Up Ctrl+↑, Move Rung Down Ctrl+↓.
  • View — Ladder Properties…, I/O Beside the Ladder, Chassis Panel, I/O Tags on Hover (3D), Wrap Rungs, Controller Organizer, Output, Simulator, Quick Watch Alt+3, Quick Watch: Floating Window, Quick Watch: Docked at the Bottom (next to Cross Reference), Cross Reference Page, Tag Descriptions in Ladder, Highlight Power Flow (not in Logix), Lock Parts in Place (no dragging in the scene; tap or click to select), Full Screen (no window frame, controller panel on one line), Tablet Layout (finger-sized controls; automatic on a touch screen), Tablet Layout: automatic, Phone Layout (in-house preview, narrow screens only).
  • Logic — New Program…, New Routine…, Verify Routine, Verify Controller, Accept Rung Text (Enter), Cancel Rung Text (Esc).
  • Communications — Go Offline, Download…, Upload…, Require a download to go online, Program Mode, Run Mode, Test Mode, Bridge & Tools, Start Bridge, Socket Bridge Settings…, Clear Faults, I/O Forcing: Enable All, I/O Forcing: Disable All, I/O Forcing: Remove All, Controller Properties….
  • Tools — Inject Machine Fault…, Fault Drill…, Scale Terminal…, Code Reader Screen…, Clear Machine Faults, Create Alias Tags for Wired I/O, Add-On Instruction Library…, New Module from EDS File…, New Generic EtherNet/IP Module…, New EtherNet/IP Device (drive, remote I/O)…, New Remote Controller (produced / consumed tags)…, Clear Tag Values (reset timers, counters, bits).
  • Window — New Trend…, Reset Tab Order, Reset Pane Sizes, Maximize Document, Simulator Docked Above, SimView (the simulator beside the ladder), Simulator as Document Tab, Open Bridge & Tools, Open MainRoutine, Open Controller Tags, Open I/O Monitor, Open Operator View, Open Cross Reference, Open Data Table, Quick Watch Alt+3, Open Simulator.
  • Help — Take the Tour (the tabs, the logic, the simulator), My Progress, Start Page, Bench Files: Level 11 Cards (STEP, print)…, Bench Files: Card Hopper (STEP, STL, 3MF)…, Guided Mode: Build the Bottle Line, Updates: What Is New (v2.02), Search Help and Project…, Glossary, Add-On Instructions, Download and Upload, Online Edits, Structured Text, Trends, Bridge & Tools, Rung Text Syntax, Level Brief and Scoring, About.
  • Theme — Slate (default), Classic (the look before v2.0), Logix Designer Blue, Graphite (control room, the dark frame), Blueprint (the engineering sheet), Dark (the whole workstation dark, the ladder on dark paper), High contrast, Holiday splash: automatic (Thanksgiving week), Holiday splash: Thanksgiving always, Holiday splash: off, Splash: the day sheet, always (white), Splash: the night sheet after dark (19:00 to 06:00), Preview the Thanksgiving splash, HMI style: high performance (ISA-101: grey, colour only for alarms), HMI style: classic colour, 3D plant: day shift, 3D plant: night shift (the windows dark), 3D graphics: High (ambient occlusion, glow on lamps, fine shadows), 3D graphics: Medium (textured surfaces, sky, sharp shadows), 3D graphics: Low (the light renderer: phones, older PCs), 3D graphics: Off (Top-down and Side only), 3D graphics: step down by itself when slow.
  • Guided — Start: Build the Bottle Line Here, New Guided Project: Build the Bottle Line…, New Guided Project: Servo Axis (ready for Level 10)…, New Guided Project: Sample Sorter…, New Guided Project: Code Reader….

Theme sets the look of the whole workstation. Slate is the default and is what this book is printed in. Classic is the look before v2.0; Logix Designer Blue is the closest to the program it is named after; Graphite is a control room’s dark frame; Blueprint is an engineering sheet; Dark turns the whole workstation dark, the ladder on dark paper; High contrast is for a projector or a bright room. The theme changes nothing but the look.

The Controller Organizer

The tree on the left is the project. Its top-level branches, as they read in v2.02:

  • Controller LogixConnect
  • Tasks
  • I/O Configuration
  • Communications
  • Add-On Instructions
  • Watch and Cross Reference
  • Trends
  • Data Types
  • Help

Controller Tags opens the tag editor. Tasks → MainTask → MainProgram holds the routines; MainTask is continuous and scans every 20 ms, and the main routine is marked (main) and is the only one the controller calls by itself — every other routine runs only when a JSR in a running routine reaches it. Right-click a program for New Routine…, right-click a routine to rename it, set it as main or delete it. New Task… adds a periodic or event task, and the Controller Fault Handler takes a program that runs when the controller faults. The Sandbox Scene Simulator opens the machine, with the I/O Monitor and the Operator View under it. I/O Configuration → Ethernet is where EtherNet/IP devices are added (a vision camera from its EDS file, a drive, remote I/O, another controller’s produced tags), and the 1769 Bus under it is the local chassis. Then come Communications (the bridge to real hardware), Add-On Instructions, Watch and Cross Reference, Trends, Data Types and Help.

Document tabs

The Start Page is where you begin (chapter 3) and the built-in help, which this book is the long form of. A routine tab is the ladder editor. Controller Tags has Monitor and Edit views. The Sandbox Scene Simulator is the machine. Bridge & Tools is the link to real hardware. Each tab carries the same small icon as its node in the organizer, so a row of routines, tags and the simulator reads at a glance. Tabs can be dragged into any order (Window → Reset Tab Order puts them back); Maximize at the end of the row gives the document the whole window and Full screen drops the window frame too.

There are three ways to see the machine and the rungs at once. Window → Simulator Docked Above puts the machine over the ladder. Window → SimView puts it beside the ladder, which suits a wide screen. Simulator as Document Tab puts it back in its own tab. Most people settle on one of the first two and stay there.

The simulator toolbar

Left to right: the Running / Program toggle; Speed (slow the machine to watch a gate, speed it up to fill a box); New Order (a new random seed for the feeders, so the parts come in a different order); Clear Parts (removes every part, zeroes the simulator’s own counters, leaves the program’s tags alone); Reset Sim (starts over: parts gone, every device back to its starting state — tank levels, cap chute, revolver drum, counters, timers — and every controller tag back to its initial value, in Program mode, with the scene and program untouched); Zoom; Floor (the size of the floor; it grows headroom by itself when a tall device sits near its top edge); View (Top-down for laying out, Side for watching fills and caps, 3D to walk the line); Labels (name tags shown, or hidden until you hover). Palette, Properties and I/O open the three drawers that float over the scene; ? opens the help for the selected part.

Above the scene are the counters: Emitted (every part the feeders have made), then three counters that read program tags — Large_Bottle_Count, Small_Bottle_Count and Scrap_Bottle_Count by default; click one to point it at any DINT tag, and a tag that does not exist shows a dash — then Total processed (parts that reached a remover, a bin or the shredder), with lost in red only when parts have fallen off the line with nothing to land on, and the simulated clock.

The bottom panes and the tags

Errors is where Verify reports (Complete - 0 error(s), 0 warning(s) is what you want to see). The Simulator Log is the machine’s own record: every part made, filled, capped, scrapped, diverted, lost or spilled, with the device that did it and the simulated time — read it before you read your ladder when something goes wrong. Search Results, Cross Reference (every place a tag is used, click to go there) and Watch (Quick Watch: a short list of tags with live values, Alt+3) complete the set.

Full screen and the tablet

View → Full Screen, or the Full screen button at the end of the tab row, drops the window title bar and folds the controller panel onto one line (key switch, Controller OK, No Forces, Energy Storage OK, No Edits, I/O OK, the path and the scan), so the document gets the height. View → Tablet Layout makes the controls finger-sized; it comes on by itself on a touch screen. On a tablet the palette, the properties pane and the I/O panel are drawers over the scene, closed to start and opened from the bar under the scene.

On a phone

The phone layout has a bottom bar (Start, Ladder, Tags, Sim, HMI, Output, and the mode button) and a bar under the scene (Zoom out, Zoom in, Fit, 100 %, I/O, Scene). The Scene sheet carries what the small screen has no toolbar room for: the View, the Floor, name tags, the background, Clear Parts and Reset Sim.

A big machine does not fit a phone’s width, so on a phone a row of chips runs across the top of the simulator: the station bar. All fits every device on the screen, small; each other chip takes you to one part of the machine, zoomed to fill the screen, in Program or Run mode. The inspection line names its stations (Feeder, Filler, Camera, Gate, Tray…); a scene without names gets its biggest machines by name. Then come the controls: a panel with its buttons is one stop, each HMI another, so START and STOP and every terminal are one tap away. The row scrolls sideways; the chip you are on is lit, and pinching or dragging the view leaves it.

Try it: run the inspection line from a phone

Open File → New Project → Inspection line on a phone, go to Run and press START on the console. Tap Feeder and watch a card drop onto the track; tap Camera and catch the PASS or FAIL; tap All to see the trays going down the conveyors.

Watch for

All on a big scene is small by design: it is a map, not a working view. Use it to see where things are, then tap the station you want to work at.
